learningObjectives.title: A major city in an LIC/NEE
Urban change in a UK city

questions.q: Which statement best defines urbanisation?
options: An increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities
The movement of people from one country to another
The growth in the total population of a country
The spread of a city outwards into the surrounding countryside
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the increasing share of a country's population that lives in urban areas rather than rural ones.

questions.q: A megacity is usually defined as an urban area with a population of over:
options: Over 1 million people
Over 5 million people
Over 10 million people
Over 20 million people
questions.explain: A megacity is an urban area with a population of more than 10 million people.

questions.q: Roughly what share of the world's population now lives in urban areas?
options: About one quarter
About one third
More than half
Almost all
questions.explain: More than half of the world's population now lives in urban areas, and the proportion is rising.

questions.q: Which of the following is a pull factor encouraging rural-urban migration?
options: Drought and crop failure in the countryside
Better-paid jobs available in the city
Lack of services in rural areas
Farm mechanisation reducing rural work
questions.explain: Pull factors attract people to cities, such as the prospect of better-paid employment.

questions.q: In many LIC/NEE cities, unplanned areas of housing built illegally by residents on the edge of or within the city are known as:
options: Squatter settlements
Green belts
Central business districts
Commuter villages
questions.explain: Squatter settlements (also called slums or favelas) are informal, often illegally built areas of poor-quality housing.

questions.q: Natural increase in a population occurs when:
options: The birth rate is higher than the death rate
The death rate is higher than the birth rate
Immigration is higher than emigration
The birth rate is equal to the death rate
questions.explain: Natural increase happens when births exceed deaths, adding to urban population growth.

questions.q: Why is urbanisation generally happening faster in LICs and NEEs than in HICs?
options: High rural-urban migration combined with high natural increase
Falling birth rates and an ageing population
People moving out of cities to rural areas
A decline in industry and employment
questions.explain: Rapid urbanisation in LICs/NEEs results from large-scale rural-urban migration plus high rates of natural increase.

questions.q: The sustainable community BedZED in London takes its name from:
options: Beddington Zero Energy Development
British Eco Design Zone
Bristol Environmental Development
Better Environment and Design
questions.explain: BedZED stands for the Beddington Zero Energy Development, a low-carbon sustainable housing scheme.

questions.q: What is a key aim of creating green space in sustainable cities?
options: To improve quality of life and provide areas for recreation and wildlife
To increase the amount of land available for factories
To reduce the cost of building new roads
To encourage more people to drive into the city
questions.explain: Green space improves well-being, supports habitats and gives residents places for recreation.

questions.q: Deindustrialisation in many UK cities has mainly led to:
options: The decline of manufacturing industry and a loss of jobs
A rapid growth in factory employment
An increase in farming in city centres
A fall in the total population of the UK
questions.explain: Deindustrialisation is the decline of manufacturing, causing job losses and often derelict industrial land.

questions.q: Urban regeneration in a UK city usually involves:
options: Improving run-down areas by investing in housing, jobs and infrastructure
Demolishing the whole city and starting again elsewhere
Moving all residents permanently to the countryside
Banning all new building in the city
questions.explain: Regeneration reinvests in declining urban areas to improve housing, employment and the environment.

questions.q: A brownfield site is best described as:
options: Land that has previously been built on and is available for redevelopment
Land that has never been built on, on the edge of a city
Protected countryside surrounding a city
Farmland used to grow crops
questions.explain: Brownfield sites are previously developed, often derelict, urban land that can be reused.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an integrated transport system?
options: Linking different forms of public transport to make journeys easier and cut car use
Building more motorways to encourage car travel
Removing all buses and trains from a city
Charging people to walk in the city centre
questions.explain: Integrated transport connects buses, trains and other modes so journeys are smooth, reducing congestion and pollution.

questions.q: Which of these is a common challenge faced by people living in squatter settlements in LIC/NEE cities?
options: A lack of clean water, sanitation and secure housing
Too many well-paid formal jobs
An oversupply of high-quality services
Very low population density
questions.explain: Squatter settlements often lack clean water, proper sanitation, electricity and legally secure housing.

questions.q: Which of the following is a way of conserving water in a sustainable city?
options: Collecting rainwater and recycling grey water
Leaving taps running to keep pipes clear
Building more coal-fired power stations
Increasing the number of private cars
questions.explain: Water conservation includes harvesting rainwater and reusing grey water to reduce demand.

questions.q: Which of these is a strategy for sustainable urban living?
options: Encouraging recycling to reduce waste sent to landfill
Increasing reliance on fossil fuels
Removing all green spaces from the city
Encouraging everyone to travel by private car
questions.explain: Reducing, reusing and recycling waste is a core strategy of sustainable urban living.

questions.q: A city suffers from heavy traffic congestion and poor air quality. Which strategy would best tackle both problems together?
options: Investing in an integrated public transport network
Building more city-centre car parks
Widening roads to allow more cars
Removing cycle lanes from the city
questions.explain: Better public transport reduces car use, easing both congestion and air pollution at the same time.

questions.q: A farmer moves to the city after a long drought destroys his crops. His decision to leave the countryside is an example of:
options: A push factor
A pull factor
Natural increase
Counter-urbanisation
questions.explain: Push factors, such as drought and crop failure, drive people away from rural areas.

questions.q: A city authority gives squatter-settlement residents legal land, basic services and building materials so they can improve their own homes. This approach is best described as:
options: A site and service (self-help) scheme
Complete slum clearance
Greenfield development
Commuting reduction
questions.explain: Site and service, or self-help, schemes support residents to upgrade their own housing with basic provision and land tenure.

questions.q: Old dockland warehouses in a UK city are converted into flats, offices and leisure facilities. This is an example of:
options: Urban regeneration
Deindustrialisation
Rural-urban migration
Natural increase
questions.explain: Reusing derelict industrial buildings for new housing and services is a form of urban regeneration.
